title: A Technical Scope must contain enough detail for an independent external team to review it with no additional context
content:
A.1.10.2.5.2.1.1 requires the completed Technical Scope Template to be published as a Sky Forum post "providing enough technical detail for **an independent external team to review the proposed changes without requiring additional context**. The Forum post creates a public record that can be challenged by the community before the action proceeds through governance."

The sufficiency standard is defined by a reader, not by a content list. That is a much harder test than a template checklist, because it fails whenever the author has relied on shared context — the tacit knowledge that makes an internal document readable to insiders and opaque to everyone else. It is precisely that shared context which prevents outside review from happening in practice.

The stated purpose sharpens it further: the point is not disclosure but *challengeability*, and specifically challengeability **before** the action proceeds. A record that becomes reviewable after execution documents a decision; one that is reviewable before it constrains a decision.

The confidentiality carve-out is narrow and directional: "Sections that, if publicly disclosed, could compromise the security of the Sky Ecosystem must be withheld from the public post and submitted directly to Core GovOps." Withheld material is not simply omitted — it is redirected to a party who must still receive it, so secrecy reduces the audience rather than the disclosure.

This standard is what makes the rest of the verification chain possible. Ecosystem Validators, Prime Spell reviewers and independent auditors all depend on being able to understand a proposed change from published material alone.
description: A.1.10.2.5.2.1.1 sets sufficiency by a stranger's ability to evaluate, and states the purpose as creating a public record challengeable before the action proceeds through governance.
